title: Practice Passage 16: How Coffee is Processed from Seed to Cup

passage.title: How Coffee is Processed from Seed to Cup
passage.sub_title: Tracing harvesting, wet pulping, tank fermentation, patio drying, parchment hulling, and drum roasting.
passage.content_html:
Paragraph A

[A1] The journey of coffee from a simple seed to a morning beverage is a complex industrial process. [A2] The coffee plant produces small red fruits known as coffee cherries. [A3] Inside each cherry, two seeds are found, which are eventually roasted to become coffee beans. [A4] Processing must begin immediately after harvesting to prevent the cherries from spoiling.

Paragraph B

[B1] The first major stage is harvesting, which is typically done by hand. [B2] Workers select only the ripe red cherries, leaving unripe green cherries on the branches. [B3] Once harvested, the cherries are transported to a processing facility where they are cleaned. [B4] Floating cherries are removed, as they are dry and of lower quality.

Paragraph C

[C1] Next, the outer skin and pulp of the cherry must be separated from the inner seeds. [C2] In the wet processing method, a machine called a pulper squeezes the cherries to remove the skin. [C3] The seeds, which are still covered in a sticky layer of mucilage, are then placed in large fermentation tanks. [C4] Fermentation breaks down the sticky mucilage layer over a period of 12 to 36 hours.

Paragraph D

[D1] After fermentation, the beans are thoroughly washed with clean water. [D2] They must then be dried to reduce their moisture content to around 11 percent. [D3] Drying is completed by spreading the beans on concrete patios under the sun or using mechanical dryers. [D4] Workers rake the beans regularly to ensure they dry evenly and prevent mold growth.

Paragraph E

[E1] The dry beans are covered in a protective paper-like layer called parchment. [E2] Before export, this parchment layer is removed by a machine during a process called hulling. [E3] The hulled beans are referred to as green coffee because of their color. [E4] These green beans are sorted by size, weight, and density to ensure uniform quality.

Paragraph F

[F1] The final critical step is roasting, which transforms the chemical properties of the green beans. [F2] Roasters use high-temperature rotating drums to heat the beans to between 200 and 240 degrees Celsius. [F3] During roasting, the beans expand, change color to brown, and release aromatic oils that create the coffee flavor. [F4] The roasted beans are cooled immediately using air or water spray.

Paragraph G

[G1] Finally, the beans are packaged in bags with one-way valves to prevent oxygen from entering while allowing carbon dioxide to escape. [G2] Consumers grind the beans and brew them with hot water, releasing the rich flavors. [G3] This sequential process demonstrates the care required to produce high-quality coffee. [G4] Understanding this flow highlights the connection between agriculture, manufacturing, and consumer enjoyment.
